summary: This work reveals that time-varying external flux threading a SQUID loop induces cross-voltage coupling to capacitively linked qubits through an inherent flux crosstalk mechanism, analogous to Faraday induction. This effect enables fast single-qubit gates via the coupler element in tunable-coupler architectures, potentially eliminating dedicated microwave control lines per qubit.
motivation: Scaling superconducting qubit systems requires reducing wiring complexity and crosstalk, as each qubit currently needs separate microwave XY control and flux bias lines. While flux tunability enables high-fidelity entangling gates, it also introduces unwanted flux coupling between nominally independent bias lines.
method: Circuit theory with time-dependent external fluxes is rigorously applied to capacitively coupled tunable transmons using node-flux formulation and irrotational gauge. For a three-transmon tunable coupler with sinusoidally modulated coupler flux $g(t) = A \cos(\omega_d t - \gamma)$, the Hamiltonian is derived showing drive terms $V_j(t)$ on qubits $j = 1, 2$ with strengths proportional to $D_j = E_{\mathrm{eff},j} J_1(\beta_j A)$, where $\beta_j = [\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{e}_c]_j$.
result: Simulations of coupler-driven X gates with $E_J/2\pi = 10$–12 GHz achieve gate times of order 20 ns with fidelities exceeding 99.9% at the coherent error level; leakage is characterized by $\beta_j A \approx 10^{-3}$ yielding drive strengths $\Omega_p$ of tens of MHz, compared to negligible strengths without inherent crosstalk. Main errors are qubit-2 phase errors and $ZZ$ cross-Kerr coupling, both addressable via pulse shaping and alternative coupler geometries.
